summary: BBN explains the sizes of TIP message buffers in response to complaints that they were too small. It gives buffer sizes by device number in each direction and explains how users can set the TIP to send full-length messages.

eli5.summary: People said the network box's mail bags were too small, so the maker lists the bag sizes and shows how to fill them.

questions: how to optimize tip message length
subtitle: Explaining why TIP message buffers vary by device and how to use them

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET users complained that the Terminal Interface Processor (TIP) message buffers were too small, limiting how much data could be sent in each message.
tldr.mechanism: The TIP provides different buffer sizes for different device ports, with larger buffers for lower-numbered devices. Users can configure the TIP to send messages on every character, at line breaks, or after a certain number of characters to control buffer usage.
tldr.outcome: By choosing appropriate TIP parameters and lower-numbered ports, users can maximize message size and efficiency within the constraints of fixed total buffer space.

today: RFC 297 explains early ARPANET infrastructure constraints. The TIP's fixed buffer allocation reflects design trade-offs between flexibility and memory efficiency that were common in early network terminals.

sections.title: Buffer Sizing on the TIP
sections.content:
The Terminal Interface Processor (TIP) receives complaints about message buffer size, but the actual buffer sizes are not as extreme as the complaints suggest. For messages from a TIP to another host, buffer sizes range from 64 characters for device ports 1-2 down to 6 characters for port 63. For messages from a host back to a TIP, sizes range from 96 characters for port 1 down to 8 characters for ports 36-63.

The TIP double buffers its terminal output, so when a connection is made, it allocates an initial buffer amount and immediately prepares a second buffer of the same size while printing the first one.
sections.eli5: Different network ports have different sized message containers, with the smaller port numbers getting bigger containers.

sections.title: Configuring TIP Parameters
sections.content:
Users have four options for when the TIP sends messages: every single character, on line feeds or carriage returns, every nth character (where n is configurable), or the combination of the latter two. Selecting a large n value (such as 100) allows the TIP to send the longest possible messages for a given device port, filling the allocated buffer completely.

Hosts that prefer not to receive very short messages can advise their users to configure the TIP to maximize buffer length. This requires users to set parameters appropriately when connecting through the TIP.
sections.eli5: You can tell the TIP to wait and gather characters into bigger messages instead of sending them right away.

sections.title: Design Constraints
sections.content:
The sizes and quantities of each buffer in the TIP are not permanently fixed and can be changed if better distributions are suggested. However, the total amount of buffer space available is fairly fixed, as each of the 63 devices requires two output buffers and one input buffer that must come from this total.

Dynamic buffer allocation at runtime would require memory compaction and mechanisms to reclaim space from current users when new users connect. The developers estimated that implementing dynamic allocation would reduce total available buffer space by about one-fifth, making fixed allocation more practical.
sections.eli5: Instead of dynamically resizing containers, the TIP uses fixed-size bags, which is simpler and wastes less space overall.

references.text: Walden, D., "TIP Message Buffers", RFC 297, January 1972.
